_note: What is in the building, as declared by the practitioner who claims the
listing. Nobody researches these and the directory never infers them:
an amenity is present because the business ticked it, and absent because
nobody has said yet — which is not the same as 'no'.
That provenance is why this is separate from the audience taxonomy. An
audience answer needs a source URL and the words on it before it counts;
an amenity is the business's own statement about its own premises. Both
are legitimate, but mixing them would let a self-declared tick sit in a
system built on evidence.
Step-free access is DELIBERATELY not in this list. It already exists as
an audience with an evidence test attached ('States step-free,
ground-floor, lift or wheelchair access to the space itself. Never
inferred from a photograph.'). Accessibility is the last thing that
should have two sources of truth and the weaker one win.
Stored as post meta via an ACF checkbox, not as a taxonomy. A taxonomy
would mint a term archive per amenity on day one, and the directory's own
rule is that a page needs three listings before it may be indexed. When
coverage exists, promoting this to a taxonomy is a migration, not a
redesign.
Keep the list short. A form with forty checkboxes is a form nobody
finishes, and a half-finished list is worse than none: it reads as
'no showers' when it means 'nobody asked'.
